stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD FALLS 7 BPS TO 4.93% A DAY AFTER THE FED'S HAWKISH HIKE
stories.body: One day after the FOMC raised the fed funds rate a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% and signaled more tightening ahead, the 10-year Treasury yield actually retreated to 4.93% while the 2-year held near 4.39%. Stocks rallied alongside the pullback, with the S&P 500 up 0.59% and the Nasdaq 100 up 1.62%.
stories.explain: The Fed only directly sets the overnight rate; the 10-year is priced off the market's expected average path of future short rates plus a term premium, so it can move opposite the policy rate. Wednesday's hawkish hike raised the odds of front-loaded tightening, which paradoxically lowers the market's expected rate path further out if investors think aggressive near-term hikes increase the chance of slower growth or earlier cuts later — a classic bull-flattening move.

stories.headline: S&P 500, NASDAQ 100 REBOUND AS TECH LEADS RECOVERY FROM FED-DAY SELLOFF
stories.body: The S&P 500 climbed 0.59% to 7,596 and the Nasdaq 100 jumped 1.62% to 29,413, clawing back Wednesday's Fed-day losses as falling yields eased pressure on rate-sensitive growth names.
stories.explain: Wednesday's selloff was driven by discount-rate math: a hawkish Fed pushes up the rate used to value future cash flows, which hits long-duration growth and tech stocks hardest. Today's yield pullback reverses that math directly, which is why the Nasdaq 100's outsized gain today mirrors its underperformance the day before — same mechanism, opposite direction.

stories.headline: GOLD RALLIES 1.1% TO $4,364 AS REAL YIELDS PULL BACK FROM WEDNESDAY'S SPIKE
stories.body: Gold rebounded to roughly $4,364 an ounce, recovering ground lost during Wednesday's Fed-driven real-yield spike as nominal 10-year yields eased 7 bps.
stories.explain: Gold pays no coupon, so its relative attractiveness is set by real (inflation-adjusted) yields, not the fed funds rate itself. When nominal yields fall while inflation expectations stay roughly anchored, real yields decline, lowering the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset — which is exactly what's pulling gold back up today after Wednesday's spike-driven selloff.

stories.headline: WTI SLIPS TO $102 WHILE BRENT HOLDS ITS MIDDLE EAST PREMIUM NEAR $104
stories.body: WTI crude eased 0.44% to roughly $102 a barrel even as Brent stayed elevated near $103.60, with the spread reflecting an ongoing Saudi pipeline outage tied to Middle East shipping disruptions that has yet to fully resolve.
stories.explain: WTI is a domestic U.S. benchmark most sensitive to inventory data, while Brent is more exposed to international supply risk — in this case, a Saudi pipeline outage rerouting several million barrels a day away from Hormuz. As long as the outage lingers, expect Brent to keep trading at a premium to WTI regardless of what U.S. inventory reports show week to week.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX HOLDS NEAR 100 AS TRADERS PRICE THE FED'S FORWARD HIKE PATH
stories.body: The DXY was essentially flat at 100.23, consolidating just above the psychological 100 level as markets digest Wednesday's guidance that a majority of Fed officials see at least one more hike before year-end.
stories.explain: A currency's value tracks the expected interest-rate differential against other major economies, not just the most recent policy move, so the dollar's flat session here reflects a market that had already priced most of Wednesday's hawkish signal into Thursday's open. The next real catalyst is incoming inflation data — a hot print would reinforce the case for another hike and likely push the DXY higher; a soft one could unwind today's stability.

stories.headline: DUKE TOPS PRESEASON POWER 44 AS PROGRAMS RAMP UP TOWARD MIDNIGHT MADNESS
stories.body: With the 2026-27 season still weeks away, Duke was named the No. 1 team in the first major preseason power ranking, while Arizona — coming off a 36-win season and its first Final Four since 2001 — has scheduled its Midnight Madness-style kickoff event for Sept. 26.

stories.headline: DOJ OPENS CRIMINAL PROBE INTO CLIPPERS OVER ALLEGED KAWHI LEONARD SPONSORSHIP SCHEME
stories.body: The U.S. Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into whether the Clippers arranged secret sponsorship deals benefiting Kawhi Leonard in violation of the salary cap; reported potential penalties under discussion include a steep franchise fine and lost future first-round picks, though no punishment has been finalized. Separately, Portland acquired former All-Star guard Ja Morant in a trade with Memphis.

stories.headline: MAHOMES, CHIEFS HOST COLTS IN SUNDAY NIGHT PRIMETIME AFTER DOMINANT WEEK 1
stories.body: Kansas City, fresh off a lopsided Week 1 win over Denver in Mahomes' return from a knee issue, is a 6.5-point favorite hosting Indianapolis on Sunday Night Football (8:20 PM ET, NBC) after the Colts opened 0-1 with a 41-23 home loss to Baltimore.

stories.headline: NO. 2 GEORGIA VISITS ARKANSAS HEADLINES A LOADED WEEK 3 SLATE
stories.body: Week 3 opened Thursday with Pitt hosting Syracuse and continues Friday with No. 5 Miami at Wake Forest and No. 13 Texas Tech vs. No. 22 Houston, before Saturday's marquee matchup: No. 2 Georgia at Arkansas (ABC), with Arizona State facing Kansas in London the same day.

deepDive.title: Why the 10-Year Yield Fell the Day After the Fed Raised Rates
content: Yesterday the Fed hiked its policy rate for the first time in three years and Chair Warsh talked tough on inflation, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5% and hitting stocks. Today, with no new Fed action at all, the 10-year fell 7 basis points to 4.93% and both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 rallied. That split — a rate hike followed a day later by falling long-term borrowing costs — looks contradictory until you separate what the Fed actually controls from what the bond market is pricing on its own.

The Fed sets one number directly: the overnight fed funds rate. The 10-year yield is not set by the Fed at all — it's the market's own estimate of the average short-term rate it expects over the next decade, plus a term premium for the extra risk of lending long. When the Fed hikes and signals more hikes are coming, bond investors have to decide whether that front-loaded tightening raises or lowers their expectation for rates several years out. If aggressive near-term hikes are read as increasing the odds of slower growth or earlier cuts down the road, the expected average path actually falls, even though the here-and-now policy rate just rose. That's a bull-flattening move: short yields up, long yields down.

The 2004-2006 tightening cycle is the textbook case of this dynamic taking over completely. The Fed hiked the fed funds rate seventeen straight times, from 1% to 5.25%, yet the 10-year yield barely budged and at points fell — a pattern Alan Greenspan famously called a "conundrum." Bond markets simply didn't believe the hikes would stick long-term, given disinflation trends already in motion, so they refused to reprice the long end in step with the short end. Today's 54-basis-point gap between the 2-year (4.39%) and 10-year (4.93%) is nowhere near that extreme, but the underlying skepticism — will this hiking cycle actually hold — is the same force at work.

The practical takeaway: a Fed hike does not raise all borrowing costs equally. Overnight-linked costs — credit cards, HELOCs, most variable-rate debt — move almost immediately with the fed funds rate. Mortgages and corporate bonds track the 10-year far more closely, which is why a flattening curve can leave a 30-year mortgage rate roughly unchanged, or even a touch lower, the same week the Fed tightens. Watch next week's core PCE print as the real test: a soft number would validate today's long-yield pullback and likely extend it, while a hot one would force the bond market to reprice the long end back toward Wednesday's levels.
